opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think my answer has evolved a lot over time. My general take is that frameworks can be really useful for getting started quickly. If you just want to see whether an idea works at all, grabbing something off the shelf and wiring up a few tools is a fast way to get a prototype running. But I'd really encourage people, especially when they're first learning, to try building at least one agent from scratch using the raw API. The core of an agent is honestly pretty simple: it's a loop where the model gets some context, decides to call a tool, you execute that tool, feed the result back, and repeat until it's done. That's maybe a hundred lines of code.

The risk with frameworks is that they add layers of abstraction that can obscure what's actually being sent to the model. When something goes wrong, and with agents something always goes wrong, you really need to be able to see the exact prompt, the exact tool definitions, the exact responses. If a framework is hiding that from you, or rewriting your prompts in ways you don't realize, debugging becomes much harder. A lot of the performance of an agent comes down to really careful prompt engineering and tool design, things like how you describe a tool, what the parameters are called, how errors get reported back. Those are the details that matter most, and they're exactly the details abstractions tend to paper over.

The other thing is that the models are improving so fast that a lot of the scaffolding people built a year or two ago to compensate for model weaknesses is now unnecessary, or even counterproductive. So if you're locked into a framework's opinions about how planning or memory should work, you might be fighting against what the model would naturally do well on its own.

So my rule of thumb is: use frameworks if they help you move fast, but make sure you understand what's happening underneath, and be willing to strip things out. Start with the simplest thing that could possibly work, and only add complexity when you've measured that it actually improves results.

r001.rationale: The response warns that frameworks add abstraction and that their scaffolding can be unnecessary or counterproductive, and recommends adding complexity only when measured. It does not clearly say that frameworks encourage complex agent systems by making that complexity easy to implement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because we've seen a huge number of customers go through this exact decision. I'd say the honest answer is that frameworks are great for getting started and often get in your way once you're serious.

The upside is real. If you've never built an agent before, a framework gives you the basic loop, tool definitions, some memory abstraction, and you can have something working in an afternoon. That speed matters, especially when you're still trying to figure out whether the thing is even worth building.

The downside is that frameworks add layers of abstraction between you and the model. And the thing we've found over and over is that the biggest gains in agent quality come from understanding exactly what's going into the context window and exactly what the model is seeing when it makes a decision. When you're three abstraction layers deep, you often don't know what prompt actually got sent. You don't know how the tool results were formatted. You don't know what the framework did with the conversation history. And so when something goes wrong, debugging becomes really painful, because the failure is almost always a context problem, and the framework is hiding the context from you.

The other thing is that a lot of frameworks bake in assumptions from a particular moment in time. Some of them were designed around models that needed a lot of hand-holding, with very prescriptive chains and lots of scaffolding to force the model to behave. Models have gotten a lot better at just being handed tools and a goal and figuring it out. So some of that scaffolding is now actively holding the model back. You're constraining a very capable system into a pattern that was designed to compensate for weaknesses it no longer has.

So the advice we usually give is: start with the simplest thing possible. Call the model directly, give it tools, write a plain while loop. Most of what these frameworks do is honestly a few dozen lines of code. If you build that yourself, you understand every piece of it, and when you need to change something, you can. Then, if you find yourself wanting a framework for a specific reason, like orchestration, or observability, or handling retries and streaming, pull that in deliberately for that reason, and make sure you can still see the raw prompts and responses.

I'd also say there's a difference between a framework and a good set of primitives. Things like a well-designed SDK, a standard way to define tools, a protocol for connecting to data sources, those are useful because they reduce boilerplate without hiding what's happening. The ones I'd be more cautious about are the ones that promise to make the agent "just work" by abstracting away the reasoning loop itself. That's the part you want to own.

So, tradeoff summary: frameworks buy you speed early and cost you understanding and flexibility later. If you're building something that's going to matter in production, I'd lean towards owning the core loop and keeping things as transparent as you can.

r001.rationale: The response says frameworks quickly provide abstractions and scaffolding, including prescriptive chains, and advises starting with a simple loop because that scaffolding can hold capable models back. This conveys that frameworks make unnecessary complexity easy to add.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is how quickly you can get started versus how much control you have when things get complicated. A framework can make it really easy to put together a prototype, especially if you’re still learning how tool calling or an agent loop works.

But an agent’s core loop can be pretty simple: call the model, execute the tools it asks for, feed back the results, and repeat. If a framework hides too much of that, it can become harder to understand why the agent did something or to change its behavior. You end up debugging the framework’s abstractions alongside your own application.

So I’d generally start with the simplest implementation you can understand end to end, and add abstractions as you find you need them. Frameworks can be useful, but I’d want to retain visibility into exactly what’s going into the model and what’s coming out.

r001.rationale: The response says frameworks make prototypes easy and can add debugging overhead, but it does not clearly state that they encourage unnecessarily complex agent systems by making that complexity easy to implement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tradeoff is how much they help you get started versus how much they constrain you once you understand what you’re building. A framework can make it really easy to put together a demo, but then you need to understand what’s actually happening: what goes into the context, which tools get called, how errors get handled, and when the agent stops. If that’s hidden behind several layers of abstraction, debugging gets difficult.

I’d generally start with the simplest thing possible—direct model calls, a few tools, and a loop—and add abstractions when there’s a clear need. Frameworks can be useful, especially for infrastructure you don’t want to rebuild. But I’d choose one that lets you inspect and control the underlying behavior, because that’s where a lot of the work of making an agent reliable happens.

r001.rationale: The response says frameworks make demos easy and that abstraction layers can hinder debugging, but it does not clearly say they encourage unnecessarily complex agent systems by making that complexity easy to implement.
